Take the relation taught for 'Three Major Landforms' and work with: mountains = 80, plains = 500, plateaus = 120. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of land.
Explain in your own words what 'Three Major Landforms' refers to.
questions.a: Land takes three major forms: mountains rising high with steep slopes, plateaus standing as raised flat lands, and plains lying low and level; a road trip from Chhota Nagpur to Almora crosses all three.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Three Major Landforms'.
questions.a: The same journey can climb a plateau, cross a plain and wind up a mountain, meeting new life at each step.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Three Major Landforms', in plain ASCII form.
Explain in your own words what 'Life in the Mountains' refers to.
questions.a: Mountains have thin air, steep slopes and cold climate; people terrace the slopes, rear sheep or grow fruit, and mountain culture, from pilgrim routes to mountain homes, grows out of this hard, beautiful life.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Life in the Mountains'.
questions.a: Mountains both challenge and shelter: they test travel and farming yet guard rivers and forests.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Life in the Mountains' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Life on Plateaus and Plains' refers to.
questions.a: Plateaus are raised flatlands, often rich in minerals and suited to grazing or special crops, while plains, level and watered by rivers, carry the densest farms, towns and transport routes.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Life on Plateaus and Plains'.
questions.a: Flat land is easy land: plains feed and house the most people, plateaus store minerals beneath.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Life on Plateaus and Plains' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Plateaus and Plains (source: fees103.txt, Plateaus and Plains)

concepts.title: The Hymn to the Earth: Landforms in Culture

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Hymn to the Earth: Landforms in Culture' refers to.
questions.a: The chapter opens with the Atharva Veda's hymn to the Earth, which calls the land our mother bearing heights, slopes and plains; landforms are thus part of prayer and culture, not just geography.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Hymn to the Earth: Landforms in Culture'.
questions.a: Ancient verses saw the Earth as a mother to be respected, binding geography with gratitude.
